content:
You are a research assistant answering questions about a fixed set of papers.
The papers are plain-text files in your working directory. Explore them with the tools:
- bash: read-only shell (ls, grep -n, find, head, tail, wc, nl, cat, sed -n 'A,Bp')
- read(path, offset, limit): read a file with line numbers

Rules:
- Answer ONLY from text you have actually read in this session. Do not answer from memory.
- If the papers do not contain the answer, say so explicitly instead of guessing.
- When you have enough evidence, reply with your final answer and make NO tool call.
- Support every factual claim with a verbatim quote copied exactly from the source, in the form: "exact text" (file). Never paraphrase inside the quotation marks. A statement that the document(s) do not contain the requested information needs no citation.
- State only what the document(s) say. Do not add background knowledge, general advice, or your own
  conclusions. If the user asks for something the text only partly covers, answer the covered part
  and say plainly which part the document does not address.
- Do not expand abbreviations, name entities, or add details that the text itself does not give.
- Do not end with a summary that recombines earlier points ("In short", "Overall"); the points stand on their own.
- When the user describes their own situation, say what the document states that applies to it; do not
  draw a personal conclusion that the document does not state itself.
- After you give an answer, an automatic check verifies your citations. If you then receive a
  <verification> message, you are in revision mode: fix ONLY the flagged problems by calling
  edit_draft(old, new), where `old` is an exact, unique substring of your previous answer.
  Keep everything else unchanged, and reply "Done" when finished.
  Never call edit_draft before you have given an answer.

What do the main findings from the industry survey say about journalism, media, and technology companies?

In your answer, refer only to the document in the file `doc.txt`. Do not employ any outside knowledge.

1	These are the main findings from our industry survey, drawn from a strategic sample of more
     2	than 300 digital leaders from more than 50 countries and territories.
     3	• Just half (47%) of our sample of editors, CEOs, and digital executives say they are
     4	confident about the prospects for journalism in the year ahead, with around one-tenth
     5	(12%) expressing low confidence. Stated concerns relate to rising costs, declining
     6	advertising revenue, and a slowing in subscription growth – as well as increasing
     7	legal and physical harassment. Reasons to be cheerful include the hope that closely
     8	fought elections in the US and elsewhere could boost consumption and interest, albeit
     9	temporarily and with the potential for further damage to trust.
    10	• Almost two-thirds (63%) of our survey respondents say they are worried about a sharp
    11	decline in referral traffic from social media sites. Data sourced for this report from
    12	analytics provider Chartbeat shows that traffic to news sites from Facebook fell 48% in
    13	2023, with traffic from X/Twitter declining by 27%. In response to these developments,
    14	around three-quarters (77%) say they will focus more on their own direct channels in
    15	the next year, with a fifth (22%) resorting to cutting costs and a similar proportion (20%)
    16	experimenting with alternative third-party platforms.
    17	• More specifically, publishers say they’ll be putting more effort into WhatsApp (+61 net
    18	score)2 and Instagram (+39) following Meta’s decision to open up broadcast channels for
    19	publishers. Interest in video networks such as TikTok (+55) and YouTube (+44) remain
    20	strong while Google Discover is becoming a more important but volatile referral source.
    21	By contrast, publisher sentiment towards Facebook has worsened further this year (-38
    22	net score) along with X/Twitter (-39 net score).
    23	• Related to the above, the majority of our publisher respondents say they plan to create more video
    24	(+64 net score), more newsletters (+52), and more podcasts (+47), but broadly
    25	the same number of news articles – as they lean into some of the few remaining areas of audience and
    26	advertiser growth. Around half (54%) of respondents admit their companies
    27	are mostly focused on maximising attention rather than being more respectful of their audience’s
    28	time (37%).
    29	• The twin dangers of selective news avoidance and news fatigue remain a major source of concern for
    30	media companies looking to sustain interest in news from Gaza and Ukraine, amongst other difficult
    31	stories. Strategies that publishers consider very important to counter these trends include better
    32	explanation of complex stories (67%), more solutionsoriented or constructive approaches to
    33	storytelling (44%), and more inspirational human stories (43%). There was less support for
    34	commissioning more positive (21%) or entertaining (18%) news.
    35	• On the business side, publishers continue to invest in subscription and membership, with a large
    36	majority of those surveyed (80%) saying this will be an important revenue stream,
    37	ahead of both display and native advertising. Most of those operating a paid model report either a
    38	slight increase, or stable subscription numbers in the last year, despite the
    39	difficult economic outlook.
    40	• As a number of publishers aim to do lucrative licensing deals with AI platforms this year, there
    41	is little optimism that any benefits will be equally shared. In our survey a third (35%) of
    42	respondents believed that most of the money would go to big publishers.
    43	Around half (48%) felt that, at the end of the day, there would be very little money for any
    44	publisher.
    45	• Using AI for back-end news automation (56%) is considered the most important use of
    46	the technology by publisher respondents, followed by offering better recommendations
    47	(37%) and commercial uses (28%). Publishers are ambivalent about using AI for content
    48	creation, which is considered the biggest reputational risk by over half of respondents.
    49	• Experimental interfaces to the internet such as AR and VR glasses, lapel pins, and other
    50	wearable devices will be a feature of the year ahead. But existing voice activated devices
    51	such as headphones and smart speakers, as they get upgraded with AI technologies, are
    52	considered by respondents to be the most likely option (41%) to displace – or at least
    53	supplement – the smartphone in the medium term.

Based on `doc.txt`, the main findings from the industry survey (drawn from "a strategic sample of more than 300 digital leaders from more than 50 countries and territories") are:

**Confidence in journalism**
- "Just half (47%) of our sample of editors, CEOs, and digital executives say they are confident about the prospects for journalism in the year ahead, with around one-tenth (12%) expressing low confidence."
- "Stated concerns relate to rising costs, declining advertising revenue, and a slowing in subscription growth – as well as increasing legal and physical harassment."
- "Reasons to be cheerful include the hope that closely fought elections in the US and elsewhere could boost consumption and interest, albeit temporarily and with the potential for further damage to trust."

**Referral traffic from social media**
- "Almost two-thirds (63%) of our survey respondents say they are worried about a sharp decline in referral traffic from social media sites."
- "traffic to news sites from Facebook fell 48% in 2023, with traffic from X/Twitter declining by 27%."
- "around three-quarters (77%) say they will focus more on their own direct channels in the next year, with a fifth (22%) resorting to cutting costs and a similar proportion (20%) experimenting with alternative third-party platforms."
- "publishers say they'll be putting more effort into WhatsApp (+61 net score) and Instagram (+39) following Meta's decision to open up broadcast channels for publishers."
- "Interest in video networks such as TikTok (+55) and YouTube (+44) remain strong while Google Discover is becoming a more important but volatile referral source."
- "publisher sentiment towards Facebook has worsened further this year (-38 net score) along with X/Twitter (-39 net score)."

**Content production**
- "the majority of our publisher respondents say they plan to create more video (+64 net score), more newsletters (+52), and more podcasts (+47), but broadly the same number of news articles – as they lean into some of the few remaining areas of audience and advertiser growth."
- "Around half (54%) of respondents admit their companies are mostly focused on maximising attention rather than being more respectful of their audience's time (37%)."

**News avoidance and fatigue**
- "The twin dangers of selective news avoidance and news fatigue remain a major source of concern for media companies looking to sustain interest in news from Gaza and Ukraine, amongst other difficult stories."
- "Strategies that publishers consider very important to counter these trends include better explanation of complex stories (67%), more solutionsoriented or constructive approaches to storytelling (44%), and more inspirational human stories (43%)."
- "There was less support for commissioning more positive (21%) or entertaining (18%) news."

**Business/revenue**
- "publishers continue to invest in subscription and membership, with a large majority of those surveyed (80%) saying this will be an important revenue stream, ahead of both display and native advertising."
- "Most of those operating a paid model report either a slight increase, or stable subscription numbers in the last year, despite the difficult economic outlook."

**AI licensing**
- "As a number of publishers aim to do lucrative licensing deals with AI platforms this year, there is little optimism that any benefits will be equally shared."
- "a third (35%) of respondents believed that most of the money would go to big publishers."
- "Around half (48%) felt that, at the end of the day, there would be very little money for any publisher."

**AI uses**
- "Using AI for back-end news automation (56%) is considered the most important use of the technology by publisher respondents, followed by offering better recommendations (37%) and commercial uses (28%)."
- "Publishers are ambivalent about using AI for content creation, which is considered the biggest reputational risk by over half of respondents."

**New interfaces**
- "Experimental interfaces to the internet such as AR and VR glasses, lapel pins, and other wearable devices will be a feature of the year ahead."
- "existing voice activated devices such as headphones and smart speakers, as they get upgraded with AI technologies, are considered by respondents to be the most likely option (41%) to displace – or at least supplement – the smartphone in the medium term."
